text: Hiram "Hank" Williams (September 17, 1923 – January 1, 1953) was an American singer, songwriter, and musician who became an early pioneer of country music and is regarded as one of the most significant and influential musicians of the 20th century. He recorded 55 singles that reached the top 10 of the Billboard Country & Western Best Sellers chart, five of which were released posthumously, and 12 of which reached No. 1. Born in Mount Olive, Butler County, Alabama, on September 17, 1923, Williams was the third child of Jessie Lillybelle "Lillie" Skipper and Elonzo Huble "Lon" Williams, who had English and Welsh ancestry. Elonzo, a railroad engineer and former Civil War veteran, suffered severe injuries from a truck accident and was hospitalized for eight years, after which Lillie assumed full responsibility for the family. Williams was born with spina bifida occulta, which caused lifelong pain and contributed to his later alcohol and drug abuse. At age three, he sat with his mother at the Mount Olive Baptist Church, where she sang hymns that influenced his songwriting. He received his first harmonica at age six and was nicknamed "Harm" by family and "Herky" or "Skeets" by friends. In 1933, he lived with his aunt and uncle in Fountain, Alabama, where he learned basic guitar chords and listened to music at dances and churches. In 1937, after a dispute with his PE teacher, the family moved to Montgomery, Alabama, where Williams won first prize at a talent show singing "WPA Blues," using the tune of Riley Puckett's "Dissatisfied." He learned guitar from African-American blues musician Rufus "Tee-Tot" Payne, who taught him rhythm and showmanship, and later from country act Roy Acuff. Williams never learned to read or notate music, instead basing his compositions on storytelling and personal experience. In 1937, he changed his name informally from Hiram to Hank. He began performing on the sidewalk in front of the WSFA radio studio, which caught the attention of the station's producers. In 1939, he formed the Drifting Cowboys with Braxton Schuffert, Freddie Beach, and Smith "Hezzy" Adair, managed by his mother, and dropped out of school to pursue a full-time music career. His alcoholism caused him to be fired and rehired multiple times by WSFA, and band members were frequently drafted during World War II, leading to instability. In 1941, he was medically disqualified from military service due to a back injury from a rodeo fall. In 1942, WSFA fired him for "habitual drunkenness," and he met Roy Acuff, who warned him about the dangers of alcohol. He worked briefly as a shipfitter's helper at the Alabama Drydock and Shipbuilding Company and at Kaiser Shipyards in Portland, Oregon. In 1943, he met Audrey Sheppard at a medicine show in Banks, Alabama, and they married in 1944 at a Texaco gas station in Andalusia, Alabama, though the marriage was legally invalid due to a lack of required divorce period. Sheppard became his manager and helped him regain his radio show. In 1945, he returned to WSFA and published his first songbook, "Original Songs of Hank Williams," containing nine songs, including "I'm Not Coming Home Anymore" and "A Tramp on the Street." In 1946, after being rejected by the Grand Ole Opry, he auditioned for Fred Rose at WSM radio studios, who recognized his potential as a songwriter and signed him to a six-song contract with Sterling Records. His first recordings included "Wealth Won't Save Your Soul," "Calling You," "Never Again (Will I Knock on Your Door)," and "When God Comes and Gathers His Jewels" (misprinted as "When God Comes and Fathers His Jewels"). The Sterling releases were successful, leading to a deal with MGM Records in 1947. His hit single "Move It On Over" was released in 1947, and in 1948 he joined the Louisiana Hayride radio program, which brought him national exposure. In 1949, he released a cover of "Lovesick Blues," which reached number one on the Billboard Top Country & Western singles chart for four consecutive months, propelling him to stardom on the Grand Ole Opry. He made his Grand Ole Opry debut on June 11, 1949, receiving six encores, and formed the Drifting Cowboys with Bob McNett, Hillous Butrum, Jerry Rivers, and Don Helms. That year, Audrey gave birth to their son, Randall Hank Williams (Hank Williams Jr.). In 1949, he also joined the Grand Ole Opry's first European tour. That year, five of his songs ranked in the top five of the Billboard Hot Country Singles, including "Wedding Bells," "Mind Your Own Business," "You're Gonna Change (Or I'm Gonna Leave)," "My Bucket's Got a Hole in It," and "Lovesick Blues," which reached No. 1. By 1950, he earned an estimated $1,000 per show (equivalent to $13,100 in 2024). To avoid confusion with jukebox operators, he began recording as "Luke the Drifter" for moral-themed songs, many of which were recitations. The pseudonym was requested by Fred Rose to prevent customers from being misled by sermons instead of music. The material was mostly written by Williams, with at least one piece by Fred Rose and others by collaborations between Williams, Rose, and himself. The songs depicted Luke the Drifter traveling and narrating stories about relationships, injustice, and death, performed with only Williams's voice, organ, bass fiddle, and Helms' steel guitar. Around this time, he released hits such as "My Son Calls Another Man Daddy," "Why Should We Try Anymore," "Long Gone Lonesome Blues," "Why Don't You Love Me," and "I Just Don't Like This Kind of Livin'." In 1951, "Dear John" became a hit, but the B-side "Cold, Cold Heart" became one of his most recognized songs, with a pop cover by Tony Bennett staying on the charts for 27 weeks and peaking at number one. Williams's career reached a peak in the late summer of 1953, when he died on January 1, 1953, at the age of 29, from heart failure in the back seat of a car near Oak Hill, West Virginia, en route to a concert in Canton, Ohio. Despite his brief career, he is one of the most celebrated and influential musicians of the 20th century, especially in country music. Many artists have covered his songs, and he influenced Chuck Berry, Elvis Presley, Waylon Jennings, Johnny Cash, Bob Dylan, and the Rolling Stones. He was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1961, the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1970, the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987, the Native American Music Awards Hall of Fame in 1999, and gained a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. In 2010, he was posthumously awarded a Pulitzer Prize Special Citation for his "craftsmanship as a songwriter who expressed universal feelings with poignant simplicity and played a pivotal role in transforming country music into a major musical and cultural force in American life." His life and career were dramatized in the 2015 biopic I Saw the Light.

Hank Williams wrote many of his songs himself, though Fred Rose contributed at least one piece, and according to his son Wesley, some songs were collaborations between Williams, Rose, and himself. The songs portrayed Luke the Drifter traveling from place to place, narrating stories of various characters and reflecting on broken relationships, societal injustice, and death. Performances of the songs featured only Williams’s voice, an organ, a bass fiddle, and Helms’ steel guitar. In 1951, Williams released hit songs such as "My Son Calls Another Man Daddy", "Why Should We Try Anymore", "Long Gone Lonesome Blues", "Why Don't You Love Me", and "I Just Don't Like This Kind of Livin'". "Dear John" became a hit that year, but the B-side "Cold, Cold Heart" became one of his most recognized songs; a pop cover by Tony Bennett stayed on the charts for 27 weeks and reached number one. Williams’s career peaked in late summer 1951 with his Hadacol tour with Bob Hope and other actors; the weekend after the tour ended, he was photographed backstage at the Grand Ole Opry signing a motion picture deal with MGM. In October 1951, he recorded a demo titled "There's a Tear in My Beer" for friend "Big Bill" Lister, who had a successful beer drinking song and needed another; the session was conducted by Ken Nelson, and the acetate was stored at Lister’s house and later given to Hank Williams, Jr., who had a hit with it and a video showing him playing with his father in an overdubbed dream sequence. MGM Records released Williams’s debut album, Hank Williams Sings, the following month. On November 14, 1951, Williams drove with Bill Lister and the Drifting Cowboys to New York, where he appeared on CBS’s Perry Como Show; he sang "Hey Good Lookin'", and the next week Como opened the show wearing a cowboy hat and sang the same song, apologizing to Williams. On May 21, 1951, Williams was admitted to North Louisiana Sanitarium in Shreveport for treatment of alcoholism and a back problem and was released on May 24. In November 1951, he fell while hunting squirrels with fiddler Jerry Rivers in Franklin, Tennessee, aggravating his congenital spinal condition; on December 13, 1951, he underwent a spinal fusion at Vanderbilt University Hospital and was discharged against medical advice on Christmas Eve with a back brace and increased painkiller use, worsening his health. In spring 1952, Williams flew to New York twice with his band and a Grand Ole Opry troupe to appear on two episodes of The Kate Smith Evening Hour; on March 26, he performed "Hey Good Lookin'" and joined in singing "I Saw the Light"; on April 23, he performed "Cold, Cold Heart", sang a truncated "I Can't Help It (If I'm Still in Love with You)" with Anita Carter, and joined in singing "Glory Bound Train". During that year, he had a brief extramarital affair with dancer Bobbie Jett, resulting in the birth of their daughter, Jett Williams. In June 1952, he recorded "Jambalaya (On the Bayou)", "Window Shopping", "Settin' the Woods on Fire", and "I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive"; Audrey Williams divorced him that year, and the next day he recorded "You Win Again" and "I Won't Be Home No More". He met Billie Jean Jones, a girlfriend of country singer Faron Young, at the Grand Ole Opry; as a girl, Jones had lived down the street from Williams during his time with the Louisiana Hayride, and he began visiting her frequently in Shreveport, missing many Grand Ole Opry appearances. On August 11, 1952, Williams was dismissed from the Grand Ole Opry for habitual drunkenness and missing shows; he returned to Shreveport to perform on KWKH and WBAM shows and in the Louisiana Hayride, where his performances were acclaimed when sober, though his alcohol abuse led to missed appearances or poor performances. In October 1952, he married Billie Jean Jones. During his last recording session on September 23, 1952, he recorded "Kaw-Liga", "Your Cheatin' Heart", "Take These Chains from My Heart", and "I Could Never Be Ashamed of You". By the end of 1952, Williams began to have heart problems. He met Horace "Toby" Marshall in Oklahoma City, who claimed to be a doctor; Marshall had been previously convicted of forgery and released from the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in 1951; he purchased a DSC title for $25 from the Chicago School of Applied Science, requesting it be spelled "Doctor of Science and Psychology", and under the name Dr. C. W. Lemon prescribed Williams amphetamines, Seconal, chloral hydrate, and morphine, worsening his heart condition. The final concert of his 1952 tour was in Austin, Texas, at the Skyline Club on December 19. His last known public performance was in Montgomery on December 21, where he sang at a benefit for a radio announcer with polio. On December 15, 1944, Williams married Audrey Sheppard, her second marriage and his first; their son, Randall Hank Williams (now known as Hank Williams Jr.), was born on May 26, 1949. The marriage was turbulent and quickly disintegrated, and Williams developed serious issues with alcohol, morphine, and other painkillers for his spina bifida occulta-induced back pain. The couple divorced on May 29, 1952. In June 1952, Williams moved into a house on Natchez Trace and Westwood Avenue in Nashville, sharing it with singer Ray Price; Price left soon after due to Williams’s alcoholism. Following an unsuccessful tour of California and several stays in a sanatorium, Williams moved to his mother’s boardinghouse by September. A relationship with Bobbie Jett during this time resulted in the birth of daughter Jett Williams, who was born five days after Williams died. His mother adopted her, who became a ward of the state after her grandmother’s death and was later adopted and raised by an unrelated couple, not learning she was Williams’s daughter until the early 1980s. On October 18, 1952, Williams and Billie Jean Jones were married by a justice of the peace in Minden, Louisiana; the next day, two public ceremonies were held at the New Orleans Civic Auditorium, where 14,000 seats were sold for each. After Williams’s death, a judge ruled the wedding invalid because Jones’ divorce had not been finalized until 11 days after the marriage; his first wife and mother pursued the matter for years. A man named Lewis Fitzgerald (born 1943) claimed to be Williams’s illegitimate son; he was the son of Marie McNeil, Williams’s cousin. Fitzgerald was interviewed and suggested that Lillie Williams operated a brothel at her boarding house in Montgomery; a family friend denied the claims, but singer Billy Walker claimed Williams mentioned men being led upstairs. Williams was scheduled to perform at the Municipal Auditorium in Charleston, West Virginia, on New Year’s Eve, December 31, 1952; advance ticket sales totaled $3,000. Due to a snowstorm in Montgomery, he could not fly and hired college student Charles Carr to drive him. On December 30, Williams and Carr stopped at the Redmont Hotel in Birmingham, Alabama; the next morning they continued to Fort Payne, then to Knoxville, Tennessee. Williams and Carr then took a flight to Charleston, but the plane returned to Knoxville due to bad weather. Back in Knoxville, they arrived at the Andrew Johnson Hotel, and Carr requested a doctor for Williams, who had consumed chloral hydrate and alcohol; Dr. P. H. Cardwell injected him with two shots of vitamin B12 containing a quarter-grain of morphine. Carr and Williams checked out, but the porters had to carry Williams to the car; Carr noted severe hiccups, while porters said he made a coughing sound twice. Carr spoke with Toby Marshall, who informed him on behalf of tour promoter A.V. Bamford that the Charleston show was cancelled and ordered him to drive Williams to Canton, Ohio, for a New Year’s Day concert. Around midnight on January 1, 1953, the two crossed into Bristol, Virginia, then drove past the state line into West Virginia, stopping in Hilltop at the Skyline Drive-in restaurant, where Carr asked for a relief driver; driver Don Surface left with Carr and Williams. They drove until they stopped for fuel and coffee at a gas station in Oak Hill, West Virginia, where they realized Williams had been dead for a long time and rigor mortis had set in. The station owner called the local police chief. Dr. Ivan Malinin performed the autopsy at the Tyree Funeral House and found hemorrhages in the heart and neck, pronouncing the cause of death as "acute rt. ventricular dilation"; he also noted Williams had been severely beaten and kicked in the groin recently (during a fight in a Montgomery bar a few days earlier), and local magistrate Virgil F. Lyons ordered an inquest due to a visible welt on his head. That evening in Canton, when Williams’s death was announced, a few people laughed, thinking it was a joke; Akron deejay Cliff Rodgers assured the crowd it was real, and when Hawkshaw Hawkins and others began singing "I Saw the Light", the crowd joined in. On January 2, Williams’s body was transported to Montgomery, Alabama, where it was placed in a silver casket displayed at his mother’s boarding house for two days. His funeral was on January 4 at the Montgomery Auditorium, with his casket on a flower-covered stage; mourners came from across the South and beyond; an estimated 15,000 to 25,000 were outside, and 2,750 inside, with about 200 black mourners on the balcony. Hundreds passed by the casket; backed by the Drifting Cowboys, Roy Acuff, Ernest Tubb, and Red Foley performed "I Saw the Light", "Beyond the Sunset", and "Peace in the Valley". Williams’s remains are interred at the Oakwood Annex in Montgomery. In late January 1953, MGM Records reduced their planned releases from 12 to 6 records for the month to meet demand for Williams’s music; the back orders were expected to cover their Bloomfield, New Jersey, pressing plant until April 1953. The label received 3,000 direct requests for pictures of the singer, combined with distributor requests, leading to outsourcing of printing and shipping. According to Acuff-Rose Music, sales from the two Williams song folios jumped from 700 per week to 5,000 in three weeks. Williams’s final single, released in November 1952 while he was alive, was "I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive". "Your Cheatin' Heart", written and recorded in September 1952, was released in late January 1953 after his death; it reached No. 1 on the country charts for six weeks, backed by "Kaw-Liga". "Take These Chains From My Heart" was released in April 1953 and reached No. 1; "I Won't Be Home No More" reached No. 4 in July, and "Weary Blues From Waitin'" reached No. 7. The Country Music Hall of Fame stated that Williams "set the agenda for contemporary country songcraft" and established the "standard by which success is measured in country music". Encyclopædia Britannica considers him "country music's first superstar" and an "immensely talented songwriter and an impassioned vocalist". The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame praised the "straightforward approach" of his songs as "brutally honest" and written in the "language of the everyman". To AllMusic, Williams "established the rules for all the country performers who followed him and, in the process, much of popular music". Entertainment Weekly’s TV critic Ken Tucker wrote that despite being a pop-culture titan and "father of country music", Williams was possibly the least likable figure in modern music, reeking of self-pity and filled with anger and misogyny, and was a master of spite. Hank Williams, Jr. wrote in his autobiography that tributes made it seem as if the entire city of Nashville kissed him while alive, though he was despised and envied while alive and became a saint after death. Alabama governor Gordon Persons officially proclaimed September 21 "Hank Williams Day". The first celebration in 1954 featured the unveiling of a monument at the Cramton Bowl, later placed at Williams’s gravesite; the ceremony included Ferlin Husky interpreting "I Saw the Light". Williams had 11 number one country hits in his career ("Lovesick Blues", "Long Gone Lonesome Blues", "Why Don't You Love Me", "Moanin' the Blues", "Cold, Cold Heart", "Hey, Good Lookin'", "Jambalaya (On the Bayou)", "I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive", "Kaw-Liga", "Your Cheatin' Heart", and "Take These Chains from My Heart"), as well as many other top 10 hits. Many artists of the 1950s and 1960s, including Elvis Presley, the Beatles, Bob Dylan, George Jones, Tammy Wynette, Jerry Lee Lewis, Merle Haggard, Gene Vincent, Ricky Nelson, and Conway Twitty, were influenced by Williams. Downbeat magazine voted him the most popular country and Western performer of all time the year after his death. On February 8, 1960, Williams’s star was placed at 6400 Hollywood Boulevard on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. He was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1961 and into the Alabama Music Hall of Fame in 1985. In 1964, the biographical film Your Cheatin' Heart starring George Hamilton as Williams was released. The American Truckers Benevolent Association voted "Your Cheatin' Heart" their favorite record of all time in the 1978 Truck Drivers' Country Music Awards. In 1987, he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame under the category "Early Influence" and received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award. He was ranked second in CMT’s 40 Greatest Men of Country Music in 2003, behind only Johnny Cash, who recorded "The Night Hank Williams Came To Town"; his son, Hank Jr., was also ranked on the list. Canadian singer Sneezy Waters performed as Williams in the stage play Hank Williams: The Show He Never Gave.

Hank Williams was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1961 and into the Alabama Music Hall of Fame in 1985. In 1964, the biographical film *Your Cheatin' Heart*, starring George Hamilton as Williams, was released. The American Truckers Benevolent Association voted "Your Cheatin' Heart" as their favorite record of all time in the fourth annual Truck Drivers' Country Music Awards in 1978. In 1987, he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame under the category "Early Influence" and received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award. He was ranked second in CMT's 40 Greatest Men of Country Music in 2003, behind only Johnny Cash, who recorded the song "The Night Hank Williams Came To Town," and his son, Hank Jr., was also ranked on the list. Canadian singer Sneezy Waters performed as Williams in the stage play *Hank Williams: The Show He Never Gave*, and a 1980 television movie adaptation starring Waters was produced. In 2004, Rolling Stone ranked him number 74 on its list of the 100 Greatest Artists of All Time. In 2005, the BBC documentary series *Arena* featured an episode on Williams. In 2010, his 1949 MGM number one hit "Lovesick Blues" was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, and *Hank Williams: The Complete Mother's Best Recordings...Plus!* received a Grammy nomination for Best Historical Album. In 1999, Williams was inducted into the Native American Music Hall of Fame. On April 12, 2010, the Pulitzer Prize Board awarded him a posthumous special citation for his craftsmanship as a songwriter who expressed universal feelings with poignant simplicity and played a pivotal role in transforming country music into a major musical and cultural force in American life. Several of Williams's descendants became musicians: son Hank Williams Jr., daughter Jett Williams, grandsons Hank Williams III and Sam Williams, and granddaughters Hilary Williams and Holly Williams are also country musicians. In July 2020, his granddaughter Katherine (Hank Jr.'s daughter) died in a car crash at the age of 27. His great-grandson Coleman Finchum, son of Hank Williams III, released his debut single credited to IV and the Strange Band in 2021. Meanwhile, Lewis Fitzgerald's son Ricky billed himself as Hank Williams IV following his father's claim of being Williams's son. On road trips, Williams carried a brown leather briefcase with notebooks containing song lyrics and musings; after his death, sixty-six unpublished songs from four notebooks were stored in a fireproof vault at Acuff-Rose Publications in Nashville and later moved to Sony ATV Music in 2002. After the 2001 tribute album *Hank Williams: Timeless* won a Grammy for country album of the year, A&R executive Mary Martin consulted about other projects using Williams's archive. Bob Dylan was given the first opportunity to perform 12 songs for a CD compilation and approached Holly Williams at a show, giving her a sheaf of lyrics he wanted her to read; she recognized them as her grandfather's work and later learned he had considered cutting an entire album or having other artists perform them. She heard nothing more until Mary Martin revived the project and contacted her publishing company. The resulting album, *The Lost Notebooks of Hank Williams*, included contributions from Bob Dylan, Holly Williams, Alan Jackson, Jack White, Jakob Dylan, Lucinda Williams, Norah Jones, Vince Gill, Rodney Crowell, Patty Loveless, Levon Helm, Sheryl Crow, and Merle Haggard, and was released on October 4, 2011. Material originally intended for radio broadcasts during Williams's tours or for distribution to radio stations resurfaced over the years. In 1993, a double-disc set of recordings from the Health & Happiness Show, broadcast in 1949 for the promotion of Hadacol, was released and later re-released in 2011 as *Hank Williams: The Legend Begins*, including unreleased songs "Fan It" and "Alexander's Ragtime Band" recorded at age 15, homemade recordings of him singing "Freight Train Blues," "New San Antonio Rose," "St. Louis Blues," and "Greenback Dollar" at age 18, and a 1951 March of Dimes recording. In May 2014, recordings of The Garden Spot Programs from 1950, a series of publicity segments for Naughton Farms, were released after being found by collector George Gimarc at KSIB in Creston, Iowa. Gimarc contacted Williams's daughter Jett and music historian Colin Escott, and the material was restored and remastered by Michael Graves and released by Omnivore Recordings, winning a Grammy for Best Historical Album. Williams was portrayed by English actor Tom Hiddleston in the 2016 biopic *I Saw the Light*, based on Colin Escott's 1994 book *Hank Williams: The Biography*. In 2023, Rolling Stone ranked Williams at No. 30 on their list of the 200 Greatest Singers of All Time. For the 100th anniversary of his birth, the Hank Williams Museum organized a three-day event in Montgomery featuring concerts at the Davis Theater at Troy University and a wreath-laying ceremony at Williams's graveside on September 17, 2023, which was proclaimed Hank Williams Day. In Nashville, the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum organized a concert featuring Rodney Crowell and Williams's grandchildren Holly, Hillary, and Sam. Billboard commented that Williams was a "breakthrough songwriter" who "remains a mythological figure." Williams died without leaving a will. In May 1953, Audrey Williams filed a lawsuit against MGM Records and Acuff-Rose demanding half the royalties from Hank Williams's records, as he had an agreement with his first wife for half the royalties, but there was no clarification about its validity after his death. Because Williams left no will, the disposition of the remaining 50 percent was uncertain, involving his second wife Billie Jean Horton, his mother, and his sister. At the time of his death, his estate was estimated at US$13,329.25 (equivalent to $156,700 in 2024). Lilly Williams considered Billie Jean's marriage to her son doubtful and filed for control of the estate. Billie Jean's lawyer argued that under Louisiana law, the marriage was legal because she married "in good faith" ten days before finalizing her divorce to Harrison Eshlimar. Doubting the legality in Tennessee and Alabama, Lilly Williams and her lawyers made offers to settle out of court with Billie Jean that reached a final of US$30,000. On August 19, 1953, Billie Jean signed an agreement accepting the money, which required her to stop billing herself as "Mrs. Hank Williams," reveal the location of Williams's Tennessee Walking Horse, and return a saddle and three suitcases; with the agreement, Lilly became the legal guardian of the estate on behalf of Hank Williams Jr. Soon after giving birth, Bobbie Jett left her and Williams's daughter at Lilly's boardinghouse. Williams's mother expressed her intention to adopt the child to the Montgomery County Department of Public Welfare in January 1953, and although Irene Williams opposed the adoption, she was granted custody and renamed the child "Cathy." Upon Lilly's death in 1955, Irene Williams assumed control of the estate and became the legal guardian of Williams's son, refusing to adopt Cathy. Irene attempted to contact Cathy's mother, Bobbie Jett, who refused to take the child because her husband was unaware of the daughter's existence. Cathy was then put up for adoption and granted money from the estate of Lilly Williams to be paid at age 21. In 1963, Wesley Rose contacted Irene regarding copyright renewals with Acuff-Rose and offered US$25,000 (equivalent to $256,800 in 2024), which Irene accepted to prevent Cathy from making a claim in the future. In 1966, an Alabama judge determined that Irene Williams held guardianship of the estate and confirmed the copyright renewal deal. Cathy's adoptive parents refused to contest the ruling. In 1967, Hank Williams Jr. was declared the only heir to the estate by a second judge. In 1969, after Irene was arrested and sentenced to jail for cocaine possession in Texas, the guardianship was transferred to lawyer Robert Stewart, and Hank Williams Jr. reached legal adulthood in 1970. On October 22, 1975, a federal judge in Atlanta ruled that Billie Jean Horton was Williams's common-law wife and that part of the copyright renewals belonged to her. At age 21, Cathy learned she was Hank Williams's biological daughter. In 1981, she found her half-siblings in California and learned of a 1952 contract between her parents recognizing her as Williams's daughter, and that court decisions in the 1960s ignored her existence. After a Supreme Court of Alabama decision in 1989, she was recognized as an heir to the estate and later changed her name to Jett Williams. In 1951, Williams hosted a 15-minute show for Mother's Best Flour on WSM radio, with some shows recorded for playback during his tours. During the mid-1960s, WSM staff photographer Les Leverett rescued acetates thrown away by the station, which were later duplicated. In the 1980s, he shared the acetates with Williams's former band member Jerry Rivers. A decade later, Leverett made a deal with former Drifting Cowboy Hillous Brutum, who did not appear on the recordings, for a commercial release. The Legacy Entertainment Group, based in Brentwood, Tennessee, was sued by PolyGram and Williams's heirs in 1997 to block the release. While the original acetates went to Jett Williams, the Legacy Entertainment Group's lawyer claimed ownership and attempted to prevent the heirs from releasing the recordings. Leverett stated that the original acetates did not belong to Brutum and that the two had made a deal to share profits from the planned Legacy release. Universal Music Group, parent of PolyGram, then claimed ownership of the shows. In January 2006, the Tennessee Court of Appeals upheld a lower court ruling that Williams's heirs—Hank Williams Jr. and Jett Williams—have sole rights to sell his recordings. In 2008, Time-Life released *Unreleased Recordings*, a selection of numbers from the Mother's Best Flour shows. In 2010, the company released a 15-CD box-set containing all the recordings remastered by sound engineer Joe Palmaccio, entitled *The Complete Mother's Best Recordings...Plus!*.† Honorary former member; was scheduled to be invited, but died before the invitation was extended.
